grades.quote: When an attempt is made to execute a privileged instruction within a virtual machine, a trap to the VMM occurs, whether the virtual machine is executing operating system code or application code, because the hardware is in user mode in either case. However, the VMM knows whether the virtual machine is in simulated kernel mode or simulated user mode and responds accordingly.
grades.reason: Directly explains trap-and-emulate. The guest runs in hardware user mode, so privileged instructions trap to the VMM. The VMM must then either simulate the instruction (simulated kernel mode) or simulate the trap into the guest OS handler (simulated user mode). This shows why interception is needed to give correct guest behavior.

grades.quote: Part (b) of Figure 7.19 on page 316 shows how a hardware-level trap to the VMM is used to simulate a trap to the operating system running within a virtual machine.

grades.quote: The baseline privileged architecture is designed to simplify the use of classic virtualization techniques, where a guest OS is run at user-level, as the few privileged instructions can be easily detected and trapped. The hypervisor extension improves virtualization performance by reducing the frequency of these traps.
grades.reason: Gives a useful part of the answer. In classic virtualization the guest OS runs at user level, so its few privileged instructions can be detected and trapped. The passage also says the H extension reduces how often these traps occur. It does not fully explain why the VMM must emulate them.
